video_title: Revisiting the China Shock (with Joseph Francis) 11/2/26
gist: Economic historian Joseph Francis argues the famous Autor-Dorn-Hanson 'China shock' findings are fragile: Borusyak-Hull-Jaravel's corrections halve the manufacturing-employment effect and, per their buried online appendix, erase the living-standards effects. He and Russ Roberts contend that the narrative nonetheless underpins a decade of bipartisan US protectionism, and that weak econometric incentives and opaque peer review let such results go unchallenged.

themes.theme: China shock evidence unravels under replication

insights.claim: Between 2000 and 2010 the US lost about 6 million manufacturing jobs (roughly a one-third decline) while nominal imports from China rose from about $100 billion (~1% of GDP) to $365 billion (~2.5% of GDP).
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Baseline magnitudes: the import surge was small relative to GDP, so attributing most of the job loss to China requires a strong causal case.
insights.quote: the United States lost about 6 million uh jobs in manufacturing which is about a a decline of about a third

insights.claim: Autor, Dorn and Hanson (ADH) instrumented US imports from China with Chinese imports into about seven or eight other OECD countries (Europe, Japan) to isolate China's supply shock from US demand.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Understanding the identification strategy matters because its weaknesses are what drive the later revisions to the headline effect.
insights.quote: they used an instrumental variable um based on Chinese imports into um I think seven or eight other OECD countries

insights.claim: Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel (Review of Economic Studies, 2022) showed ADH largely compared manufacturing towns with service towns, conflating China's impact with the long-run decline of US manufacturing dating from the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Much of the measured 'China effect' may simply be secular manufacturing decline; region-level trade-exposure stories deserve skepticism.
insights.quote: a lot of the effect on the manufacturing share of employment that Otter Adal had found was basically a comparison between manufacturing towns and towns without any manufacturing

insights.claim: After adding controls that compare commuting zones with similar manufacturing intensity, the estimated effect of China exposure on the manufacturing employment share fell by about half, from roughly 0.6 to 0.3.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: The headline job-loss estimate attributed to China is likely overstated by about 2x.
insights.quote: It fell from about from about 0.6 to 0.3.

insights.claim: Roberts estimates that halving ADH's figure (originally ~25% of the 1990-2007 manufacturing decline and ~45% of the 2000-2007 decline, about 1.5-2 million jobs) implies only ~700,000 to 1 million jobs attributable to China, against a workforce of roughly 135-150 million.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Recalibrates the scale of the 'China cost millions of jobs' narrative underpinning tariff policy.
insights.quote: It might only be 700,000 to 1 million rather than 1.5 to 2 million once [snorts] that correction is made.

insights.claim: Francis found that ADH's regressions cannot actually reproduce the '25% / 45%' share figures stated in their abstract.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: The most-cited statistic from the most influential trade paper may not be supported by its own regressions.
insights.quote: their regressions can't actually produce that figure

insights.claim: Page 45 of Borusyak-Hull-Jaravel's online appendix (table C.1) shows their corrections eliminate ADH's negative effects on unemployment, wages, household income and welfare transfers, yet the published article mentions this only in a footnote.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: The living-standards harm from Chinese imports, central to the protectionist case, does not survive corrected research design.
insights.quote: their corrections kind of eliminated all those effects all those negative effects on on on living standards

insights.claim: Francis speculates the appendix finding went unpublicized because young economists chasing top-five journal publications for tenure avoid upsetting senior economists; it sat unnoticed for about four years.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Academic incentives can keep inconvenient findings buried; check appendices before trusting headline results.
insights.quote: you might not want to upset senior economists if if if you want to get published in top five journals

insights.claim: ADH later published a handbook chapter incorporating some of the Borusyak et al. corrections but did not address the broader implications for living-standard effects; David Autor only thanked Francis for sending the working paper.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: The original authors have not publicly conceded the weakened findings, so the narrative persists in policy circles.

insights.claim: Peter Hull reportedly has not found errors in Francis's critique, though a separate R statistical package Francis released was criticised by Borusyak and he retracted it.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: The core critique appears to stand among the econometricians closest to the issue.

themes.theme: Deindustrialization: technology and wealth, not just China

insights.claim: Roberts argues the US manufacturing share of employment has fallen steadily since 1945 because technology lets fewer workers make more output, while manufacturing output itself remained very healthy.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Policies premised on trade-driven 'hollowing out' misdiagnose a productivity story; reshoring will not restore jobs at historical levels.
insights.quote: It's a tremendous tribute to human creativity in figuring how to make more stuff with fewer people using technology and innovation.

insights.claim: Whether falling manufacturing employment is caused by imports or by domestic innovation determines whether tariffs are justified; if technology is the driver, protection is 'barking up the wrong tree'.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Tariff regimes built on the China-shock diagnosis risk costs without the promised employment benefits.
insights.quote: otherwise you're you're barking up the wrong tree there

insights.claim: Francis's prior as an economic historian is that countries industrialize then de-industrialize as they grow wealthier and workers leave manufacturing, a wealth effect facilitated by globalization.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Deindustrialization is a structural phase of rich economies; investors should not expect policy to reverse it.
insights.quote: it's basically a wealth effect

insights.claim: Had China remained closed, Japan, Malaysia or India would probably have supplied US demand instead; China at most slightly accelerated a long-running process.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Decoupling from China likely shifts sourcing to other low-cost producers rather than bringing production home.
insights.quote: it might have been Japan, it might have been Malaysia, it might have been India supplying the American market

insights.claim: China's WTO accession and transition to capitalism was one of the most dramatic economic events ever, but the real question is how responsive the US labor market was, including workers' ability to relocate.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Labor mobility, not the shock itself, determines regional damage from trade exposure.

insights.claim: Unhealthy housing markets make it expensive to move to where the best jobs are, and lower-educated manufacturing workers may struggle to find equally attractive jobs, fueling US anger at elites.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Housing supply constraints and skill mismatch amplify the political fallout from any sectoral shock, sustaining populist trade policy.
insights.quote: If housing markets are not particularly uh healthy, it can be very expensive to move to the places where the best jobs are.

insights.claim: Francis would study deindustrialization with time-series analysis, small-scale econometrics on sub-questions (Chinese imports, other countries' imports, automation), and a holistic synthesis plus contemporary 1980s-90s debates, rather than single X-causes-Y regressions.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Single-cause empirical claims about macro trends should be discounted in favor of multi-factor analysis.

themes.theme: Political economy of blaming China for trade

insights.claim: The ADH work has been cited thousands of times and the term 'China shock' surged after 2016; it was used to prop up a decade of US policy decisions that changed America's stance on foreign trade.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: A fragile academic result underpins bipartisan protectionism; if the evidence erodes, the intellectual basis for tariffs weakens.
insights.quote: was definitely used to prop up a variety of pol policy decisions made over the last 10 years

insights.claim: Blaming China was originally a Democratic position (Nick Kristof in 2005 described elites scapegoating China); Trump brought Republicans aboard, creating an unusual bipartisan consensus.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Bipartisan anti-China trade sentiment means tariff and decoupling policies are durable regardless of election outcomes.
insights.quote: now it's kind of a bipartisan consensus there which is quite unusual

insights.claim: Francis argues the China narrative lets US politicians avoid debating harder domestic issues, continuing a long American tradition of anti-China rhetoric dating to the 19th century.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Expect China-blame to remain politically useful, sustaining trade friction beyond what economics justifies.
insights.quote: it's much easier to to blame foreigners

insights.claim: Drawing on Argentina's economic history, Francis, a self-described leftist, warns that industrial policy and protectionism are much harder to execute well than proponents assume.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Treat US industrial-policy and protectionist programs as execution-risky; Argentina is the cautionary precedent.
insights.quote: from studying Argentina, I do know that it's not as easy as it sounds

insights.claim: Globalization has long been known to create regional winners and losers (since Ohlin in the 1930s); embracing it requires compensating losers, otherwise they vote for politicians who do unwise things.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Absent compensation, trade-exposed regions drive policy volatility; political risk of trade openness is endogenous to redistribution.
insights.quote: if you're going to embrace globalization, you need to do something to compensate the losers

insights.claim: Economists shifted from confidence that trade benefits the country overall to accepting that the China shock was so large it demanded a policy response, a change Francis attributes partly to a taste for simple causal stories.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Expert consensus on trade shifted on thin evidence; consensus shifts can reverse as replication evidence accumulates.

insights.claim: Roberts argues that economists run many regressions until they find a publishable, defensible result, which he calls the wrong way to do econometrics but the way it's done.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Treat dramatic single-study empirical claims, including those driving policy, as likely overstated.
insights.quote: we run a lot of regressions till we find something that's publishable or that we think we can defend

insights.claim: The 'credibility revolution' gave economists econometric 'shiny toys' to claim X causes Y; a younger generation of econometricians is now pushing back to make results more robust.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Newer methodological work is systematically shrinking celebrated effects; expect more headline results to be revised down.
insights.quote: here's my shiny toy. Would you like to play with it?

insights.claim: Following Ed Leamer's 'Taking the Con out of Econometrics', Francis argues many economics results are fragile (disappear when specifications change) and whimsical (rest on fragile baked-in assumptions).
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
entities: taking the con out of econometrics
insights.so_what: Stress-test assumptions behind any economic study used to justify an investment or policy thesis.

insights.claim: Real-world outcomes have multiple causes, so regression techniques built to show X causes Y may poorly explain phenomena like deindustrialization, where China probably played a small role.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Beware single-factor macro narratives; multi-causal drivers mean single-lever policies underdeliver.
insights.quote: China might have had a role but it was probably quite a small role

insights.claim: The replication crisis and the file-drawer effect mean only dramatic, large results get published while null results are discarded.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Published effect sizes are biased upward; haircut academic estimates when sizing policy impacts.

insights.claim: Economics journals publish replication packages, but Francis's impression is that no one looks at them, and journals told him to send his complaints to Econ Journal Watch.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Formal transparency mechanisms in economics provide little real verification.
insights.quote: the economics journals they make all these replication packages available. Um but my impression is that no one looks at them.

insights.claim: Francis calls economics peer review a black box that is 'quite corrupt' because it isn't open: editors can override reviewers or favor friends, unlike Nature, which often publishes reviewer reports.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Opaque review means journal publication is a weak quality signal for economic research used in decision-making.
insights.quote: It it's it's quite corrupt and because it's not open.

insights.claim: The sciences have a culture of aggressive post-publication review, e.g. scientists tearing apart a Nature cancer-treatment-timing study within weeks, while in economics published results tend to be treated as law.
insights.speaker: Joseph Francis (economic historian, University of Birmingham)
insights.so_what: Economic findings lack fast error-correction, so flawed results can shape policy for years.
insights.quote: in economics when something gets into a journal it tends to be taken as kind of as as law
